inline.s: The Xiu Xin Jue (Essentials of Mind-Cultivation) says: “There are many gates to enter the Way, but to state it briefly, they do not go beyond two: sudden awakening and gradual practice.” It also says: “These two gates, sudden and gradual, are the rule of a thousand sages. All the saints above have in every case first awakened and then practiced, and by practicing attained realization. The so-called spiritual powers and transformations are unfolded through gradual nurturing, relying on awakening and practice; they are not revealed at the very moment of awakening.”

Master Guifeng says: “Recognizing that the frozen pond is entirely water, one depends on the warmth of the sun to thaw it; realizing that the common man is already the Buddha, one relies on the power of the Dharma to nurture and refine. When the ice melts, the water flows and moistens, and only then does its power to irrigate and cleanse become manifest; when delusion is exhausted, the mind becomes empty and transparent, and only then does its radiance shine forth. The spiritual powers and transformations in worldly affairs are not the work of a single day, but are gradually nurtured and manifested.”

Yangshan, instructing the assembly, said: “I now tell you plainly: do not go grasping and clinging, but simply cultivate truthfully within your own nature-sea, and do not seek the three insights and six superknowledges. Why? These are matters of the very margin of sainthood. For now, simply recognize the mind and realize the nature; once you obtain the root, do not worry about the branches. In days to come, it will be spontaneously complete and full. If you have not obtained the root, and merely learn such things with the emotions, you will never attain them; and what you do attain will not be true, and will in the end lead you into the demonic realm.”

From the above citations we can see that sudden awakening means this: when the common man is deluded, he mistakenly grasps the four elements as his body and false thinking as his mind, not knowing that his own nature is the true Dharma-body and that his own spiritual knowing is the true Buddha; forever seeking the Buddha outside the mind, running east and west, until suddenly a good-knowledge points him to the entrance, and in a single turn of the light he sees his own nature and recognizes his own mind. And this mind-nature is originally without affliction, originally without arising and ceasing, perfect and complete of itself, fully endowed of itself, in no way different from the Buddhas; and from the common man to the Buddha-stage there is no further gradation or sequence. Hence it is called sudden awakening.

Although it is called sudden awakening, yet this belongs to the side of principle; in the realm of actual practice, habitual defilements accumulated over many lives and kalpas — born and dying, clinging firmly — can by no means be suddenly eradicated. Therefore one must, relying on awakening, practice to gradually remove habitual tendencies until delusion is exhausted, and only then do spiritual powers manifest. It is absolutely not the case that spiritual powers appear at the moment of the sudden awakening to principle. Hence the cultivator must clearly understand the process, distinguish what comes first and what comes after, and must not, because of the absence of spiritual powers, doubt himself or, still more, doubt others — supposing that none of them can awaken — and so take another path and fall into a wrong way. Even if he passed through kalpas of dust he could not accomplish the Way.

Moreover, whether one has revealed spiritual powers does not suffice to show whether or not one has awakened. First, there are many kinds of supernormal powers: some are gained through esoteric practices, some through the agency of spirits and ghosts, some as a karmic reward of prior nurture, and so forth — one cannot claim that all such persons have awakened. For these powers, having some support, are not true powers, or are only semblances of power; once the physical body decays and loses its support, they vanish completely. Second, the ancients distinguished between awakening-first-then-powers and powers-first-then-awakening; one cannot say that once powers appear, one has awakened. For example, when Master Poshan of the Ming era cultivated at Tiantong, before he awakened he could already project his spirit to steal a villager's duck, playing at samadhi games. Later, when the matter came to light, Master Miyun Wu scolded him: “Your playful spiritual powers are not wanting, but you have not even dreamed of the Buddha-Dharma!” Poshan knelt and begged for instruction, and only after arduous further effort did he awaken. Coming down to modern times, the faculties of sentient beings are even poorer and their obstruction heavier; of those who would have powers first and awaken later, not one in ten thousand is to be found. Therefore we must, after awakening, practice relying on the awakening, gradually removing habits and gradually revealing powers. All the sages and patriarchs of old were without exception thus. Hence the two gates of sudden awakening and gradual practice are the norm for Buddhists, and followers of every school should practice and observe them!

Someone might say: Principle is precisely practice, and practice is precisely principle; principle and practice are not two. If principle is like sudden awakening, then practice should correspond accordingly; if in practical matters one still cannot pass through and there remain hindrances, how can it be said that one has awakened to the true principle!

Answer: Principle and practice are neither one nor different. Practice is accomplished through principle; principle is revealed through practice. Principle does not depart from practice, practice does not depart from principle; because of this non-separation, they are not different. But the true principle is formless, while its wondrous function follows conditions, responding to all things — falsely establishing empty forms that are not without shape; because of this presence and absence of form, they are not one. Now, when one has awakened, although one has clearly realized that one's own empty and still spiritual knowing is the true Buddha, yet because the habitual defilements of many lives are deep, they cannot be eradicated all at once; when meeting circumstances one still gives rise to thoughts, and before objects one can still hardly be without thought. But when thoughts arise, it is not as with the blind, who do not know that the dust-realms are originally empty, cling and grasp, wander and forget to return. Rather, when the previous thought stirs, the next thought is immediately aware and sweeps it empty. Only, compared with one who is wholly unmoved in mind, there remain traces of arising and ceasing, and the power is a little weaker. But if one can nurture and maintain it closely, constantly aware and observant, as days grow long and merit deepens, one will naturally merge it into one piece. The ox-herding practice of the patriarchs of old is precisely the model of effort after awakening.

The ancients said: Though sudden awakening makes one the equal of the Buddhas, yet the habitual tendencies of many lives are deep; the wind stops but the waves still surge, principle is revealed but thoughts still encroach. Therefore after awakening one must constantly watch. If false thoughts arise, do not follow them; reduce and reduce again until one reaches the unconditioned, and only then is it final. None of the good-knowledges under heaven who can manifest spiritual powers and transformations in their deeds have done so in a single day; they are gradually nurtured and revealed. Moreover, spiritual powers are matters of the very margin of sainthood, and in the eyes of the wise man they are not held in esteem; though they may arise, he does not wish to use them. If one has not reached the root — clear mind and seeing nature — but only seeks the branches — the manifestation of powers — not only can one not accomplish the Way, but one is bound for the demonic realm. This is something one must be careful about!

The Buddhists of today constantly measure others by spiritual powers, imagining that at the moment of awakening countless wondrous functions and spiritual powers forthwith appear, and that without such powers, though the eye of the Way be clear, one is still not awakened. Such people are indeed what one would call those who do not know root and branch, do not distinguish before and after — deluded and infatuated fools. They are themselves discouraged and do not believe in others; to cut off the Buddha-seed is nothing worse than this. How lamentable!

As for the second kind of chronic malady — holding that once one awakens all is done, with nothing to practice, nothing to attain, nothing to realize — compared with the former view that once one awakens powers appear, though it seems to have some awakening, yet because the view is not thorough, one has gone astray into a wrong path. The loss is the same as for those who have not awakened, and the harm may be even greater. For the former merely becomes self-discouraged, distrusting himself and others; but when the time and conditions arrive, he may still shatter his delusion and enter the proper track. The latter, however, believing himself to have awakened, has a deeply rooted wrong view, dispenses with later practice, and drifts on as before, sinking deeper into transmigration, with no power to extricate himself!

As said above, no-practice, no-attainment, no-realization belong to the side of principle, and are the final speech of those who have reached home; they are absolutely not reached at the moment of a single awakening. Especially for people of the present degenerate age, with poor faculties and heavy obstructions, one cannot, after awakening and without further cultivation, at once reach the state of effortless function. Those who say that there is no need to cultivate and that once one awakens all is over are either madmen or fools, and truly not to be believed.

For all sentient beings are originally endowed with the Tathagata's wisdom and virtue; only because of delusion and ignorance they do not know it, take the false as real, create karma and receive retribution, revolving through the six realms, reduced to sentient beings. Yet though in the state of a sentient being, their original nature is not lost; with a single awaking, they are no different from the Buddhas, not depending on contrived accomplishment — hence it is called no-practice. All forms are false and vain, originally empty and still, with not a single dharma — hence it is called no-attainment. At the ultimate ground even the Buddha is not established — hence it is called no-realization. But when the false habits have not yet been removed, and one clings and grasps, revolving in birth and death, one is not other than a sentient being. Therefore one must cultivate and nurture every thought, contemplate and illuminate every mind; after great awakening, with regard to evil, break evil and yet break without breaking (not clinging to marks); with regard to good, cultivate good and yet cultivate without cultivating — entering the hall and mounting the seat, returning home to sit at ease. This is what is meant by the “scholar of the unconditioned, the idle man,” and only then is it the time of no-practice, no-attainment, no-realization. If one has not reached this point and yet speaks loftily of no-practice, no-attainment, no-realization, is this not to deceive the worthy and cheat the sages, bringing grief upon oneself?
〔The expression zi yi yi qi (
yi

) meaning self-invited sorrow, means bringing trouble upon oneself, inviting one's own grief. The first yi (zi yi, to leave or bequeath) means 'to bequeath or leave behind'; the second yi means 'this'; qi means 'sorrow, grief.'

Someone might say: Sudden awakening, sudden practice, sudden realization have existed since ancient times; does such a person not indeed awaken and be done? And does such a person also need gradual practice after awakening? If such persons have existed since ancient times, surely they are not lacking even now.

Answer: Those who awaken suddenly, practice suddenly and realize suddenly cannot enter unless they are persons of the highest faculties. To speak truthfully, the reason such persons' faculties are so high and deep is that in the past they practiced relying on awakening and accumulated through gradual nurturing; now, with their karmic conditions mature, they can awaken upon hearing and complete it all at once. On the surface it seems to be sudden awakening, sudden practice, sudden realization; in fact it is likewise the case of first awakening and then practice. The ancients said: Today's sudden is also yesterday's gradual. As for the present world, students' faculties are low and mean; unless they are great bodhisattvas returning, it is truly hard for them to suddenly awaken, suddenly practice, and suddenly realize. Even if there were one or two persons of great faculties who understand a thousand things upon one hearing and complete it all at once, they still cannot be without practice, without attainment, without realization. For the ignorance and habitual defilements cannot be finished in one lifetime; and how much more so, to speak of no-practice, no-attainment, no-realization — one has long since fallen into the midst of practice, attainment, and realization.

The Xiu Xin Jue says: “The common man, from beginningless kalpa, has revolved in the six realms, firmly grasping the self-mark, with false thoughts inverted, and the seeds and habits of ignorance, long established, have become nature. Though in this life he suddenly awakens to his own nature, originally empty and still, identical with the Buddha, yet these old habits are by no means easy to cut off. Hence when he meets favorable and adverse circumstances, with anger, joy, right and wrong blazing up and ceasing, the defilement of the guest-dust is no different from before. If he does not exert the power of prajna to nurture and cultivate, how can he counter and purify it, and reach the ground of great rest and great cessation?”

Great Master Dahui Gao said: “Often those of sharp faculties, without expending much effort, settle the matter and then give rise to an attitude of ease, and do not cultivate further. As days and months grow long, they drift on as before, and inevitably fall into the cycle of transmigration. How can one, with a single period of awakening, dispense with later practice?”

Hence after awakening one must constantly observe and must not take it lightly. When a false thought suddenly arises, either a single alertness, or raising the Buddha-Recollection, until one reaches the unconditioned — only then is it final. Thus the meaning of sudden awakening and gradual practice is like the two wheels of a cart: lacking either one is insufficient.

Since sudden awakening and gradual practice are both the rule of cultivation and the bridge to the Way for Buddhists, how should one cultivate? And what difference is there from cultivation before awakening? Let me discuss this below.

(1) Cultivation after awakening cannot be spoken of uniformly; it must be determined by the depth of the student's false habits and the weight of his affliction. Those with shallow habits need no countermeasure; they merely go along with conditions, observing: when a thought arises, be aware of it; when aware, turn it to emptiness. Practicing thus from thought to thought, they naturally, little by little, attain the hundreds and thousands of samadhis. As the Xiu Xin Jue says: “Yet when one observes that delusion has no root, and thought by thought does not abide, the flowers of the three realms, like wind curling smoke, and the illusory six dusts, like soup melting ice, the defilement of the guest-dust naturally all turns into ambrosia.” If the student can thus practice from thought to thought, not forgetting to attend, holding concentration and wisdom equally, then love and hate will naturally grow faint, and wisdom will naturally grow and flourish. If the subtle continuous flow is eternally cut off, the great prajna of perfect enlightenment will shine forth alone, and then one manifests the hundreds of thousands of billions of transformation-bodies, responding to conditions in the ten directions without hindrance.

The Xiu Xin Jue says: “Though one cultivates the ten thousand practices, yet one takes non-thought as the essential. All the good-knowledges under heaven, after awakening, practice the ox-herding; though there is later cultivation, yet they have already suddenly awakened — false thoughts are originally empty, the mind-nature is originally pure. Though they cut off evil habits, there is no evil habit to cut off; though they diligently cultivate merit and wisdom, there is no merit or wisdom to cultivate; cultivating without cultivating, cutting off without cutting off — this is true cultivation and true cutting off.”

It further says: “When seeing forms and hearing sounds, just be thus (that is, when seeing forms and hearing sounds, be like a bright mirror reflecting things, like the wind passing over trees, without giving rise to other thoughts); when dressing and eating, just be thus; when relieving oneself, just be thus; when meeting people and dealing with affairs, just be thus; and even in walking, standing, sitting and lying down, whether speaking or silent, whether joyful or angry, in every moment be thus in each of these. Like an empty boat riding the waves, rising and falling with the swell, yet thought after thought not abiding; like flowing water turning the mountain, meeting bends and meeting straights, yet with the mind utterly without knowing. Today buoyant and free, tomorrow free and buoyant; following all conditions, without obstruction, without hindrance; upright and without falsity, seeing and hearing as usual — then, not a single dust standing against you, what need of the work of driving and expelling? not a single thought giving rise to emotion, no need of the power of forgetting conditions.”

Such free-flowing still knowing, being originally the cultivation of the unconditioned, is in fact equal to no cultivation. It neither requires starting a new furnace to cling to Dharma and practice, nor reserving a still contemplation, taking stillness as practice — how completely at odds with cultivation before awakening, when one did not know the why and wherefore, firmly clung to the Dharma-marks, held fast to the rituals and rules, greedily sought merit and virtue, chased after tasks, and wore the shackles and chains of a prisoner!

(2) As for those with deep habitual defilements and great power of ignorance, who among good and evil, favorable and adverse states cannot help being swayed, whose minds are not serene — for these there is indeed the work of expelling false conditions and counteracting them. In the remedial methods, if agitation predominates, one should gather the scattered mind through the concentration-power appropriate to it; if drowsiness and dullness predominate, one should contemplate emptiness through the gate of wisdom (as to what type of practice is suitable, please see the next chapter, “The Ten Methods of Cultivation”). One must cause concentration and wisdom to be held equally, stillness and movement to annul each other, and enter the unconditioned; only then is it final. The Xiu Xin Jue says: “First, through the gate of concentration gather the agitation, causing the mind not to follow conditions, to accord with original stillness; next, through the gate of wisdom awaken the drowsiness, selecting the Dharma and contemplating emptiness, according with original knowing. Use concentration to govern chaotic thought; use wisdom to govern the indeterminate. When drowsiness and agitation mutually annul, and the remedial work is ended, then in the presence of objects, every thought returns to the essential; meeting conditions, every mind accords with the Way; practicing with free-flowing spontaneity in both, one is then without affairs.”
Someone might say: Such remedial cultivation is no different from the gradual practice of the inferior faculties before awakening — then what is the point of speaking of sudden awakening?

Answer: Because such persons have poor faculties and heavy habits, deep obstruction and thick defilement; though they too awaken to the self-nature's purity and emptiness, endowed with all virtues, the same as the Buddha, yet they are unable to face conditions without arousing feeling, and encountering conditions they become stoppered; being turned about by drowsiness and agitation, they are blinded to the still and constant knowing. Without relying on the remedial work to balance drowsiness and agitation, not only can they not enter the unconditioned, but they fall into delusion after awakening. One must be careful of this.
I will cite one or two kung-an cases of falling into delusion after awakening, to serve as a warning to those who, after awakening, still do not practice earnestly.

Elder Xian long studied under Xuedou, and after obtaining the Dharma, Xuedou intended to raise him to be abbot of Jine, but Xian would not comply. Later he went out to establish a monastery and lecture, and because the Elder Yuan of Deshan surpassed Xuedou in repute and fame, he changed to acknowledge Yuan as his teacher. Having the messenger carry letters to the various mountains, the old woman before the mountain gladly asked: “For whom does Elder Xian offer incense on his first ascent to the seat?” The envoy said: “For Elder Yuan of Deshan.” The old woman cursed him, saying: “Xuedou emptied his bowels and bladder to speak Zen to you, so that you have today's station — how can you be so ungrateful and unrighteous!”

Elder Jue of Kaisheng in Hezhou first studied under the Iron-Foot Fu of Changlu, and for a long time gained nothing. Later he went to the assembly of the Fifth Patriarch Yan of Dongshan and obtained the Dharma. Going out to reside at Kaisheng, he saw Changlu's assembly flourish greatly, and so changed to succeed Fu. Not acknowledging what he had received, when he offered incense he suddenly felt his chest pounded as if beaten, and an abscess grew into a fistulous opening at the painful spot. He plugged it with a cake of frankincense, and for a long time it did not heal — and at last he died!

Abbot Qing of Shu, well known in the monasteries, one day traveled together with Master Xiu into the capital to seek the Chan Master Fayun Yuantong. When they reached Fayun, Xiu was allowed to enter the hall and take lodging, but Abbot Qing was not granted permission. Qing was staying at Zhihai, and happened to fall ill. Xiu wished to ask after him, but the gate of the mountain gave no leave; so he secretly went to Zhihai to see Qing. Qing, in turn, wrote a letter to Yuantong, alleging that Xiu had gone in and out in violation of the rules. When Yuantong learned of it, at the night assembly he scolded: “Because of friendship and righteousness he risked expulsion to ask after your illness, and you in turn write a letter accusing him — is this what an upright man and true scholar would do?” When Qing heard this, he covered his breath. The whole monastery said that Qing died after a single scolding from Yuantong.

Attendant Ping of Dayang was a worthy disciple of the Chan Master Ming'an of the Caodong school. One day the Chan Master Yaoguangzhao came to visit, and Ming'an said to him: “He who will revitalize the Caodong lineage will be either Yuan or Jue.” Zhao said: “There is Attendant Ping.” An said: “Ping's old habits are deep.” And pointed at his chest, saying: “This place is not good either.” Then he pinched the fork of his thumb, showing it, and said: “In the future Ping will die right here.” When Ming'an passed away, Ping lived at Dayang and plotted to get the gold and silver that the commandant Li Hewen had given to his teacher, not hesitating to destroy the master's reliquary stupa. Though the elders of the mountain earnestly admonished him, he would not listen. When he opened the stupa, his teacher's face and countenance were as if alive; the wood was consumed and still he sat upright. All were astonished. Ping further struck open his teacher's skull, added more oil and wood, and in a moment it was reduced to ashes. The assembly reported this to the authorities, and Ping was convicted of plotting for the objects in the stupa, and for unfilial conduct was returned to lay life. Because of his bad character, all the quarters abandoned him. Ping drifted with nothing to rely on, and later was devoured by a great tiger at a three-forked crossing. And so he could not escape Ming'an's finger-fork prophecy. How sad!

Such kung-an cases are too many to enumerate in full; they are all cases where, after awakening, one did not rely on remedial practice and earnest cultivation, and with deep-rooted habits, blinded to one's conscience, was stirred to greed by profit and forgot kindness and righteousness — thus bringing it about. Of course, a man may give play to his wicked, fierce, crafty intelligence, but how can the Dharma-protectors be without mercy toward him? That he should come to no good end is only fitting!

One must know that though one borrows remedial work to temporarily adjust the habits, yet because one has first suddenly awakened to the mind-nature being originally pure and the afflictions being originally empty, one does not cling to the Dharma to cultivate, falling into the inferior view of practice, attainment, and realization. Hence one is able to return to the essential in every thought and accord with the Way in every mind, without losing the import of sudden awakening. Conversely, if one cultivates before awakening, because one has not seen the nature, though one nurtures and cultivates from thought to thought, yet in every step one gives rise to doubt; one cannot be free and unobstructed, and at the same time clings to Dharma-marks and grabs at merit and virtue, so that birth and death remain unended. Therefore, with the same remedial methods, for one who has awakened they are like a lodging borrowed overnight — a temporary expedient; he does not fall into attachment to the Dharma, and as days and months grow long, he naturally accords with the mystery of the Way and accomplishes supreme bodhi. This is no different from the prior sharp faculties with shallow habits, cultivating without cultivating, and not cultivating while cultivating — this too must be known.

Again, take the Pure Land followers who recite the Buddha's name. Before awakening, they do not know to return to the essential in every thought, but only seek outside, cultivating with attachment to form; some, worse, cling to the mark of merit, take quantity as superior, and rush through reciting sutras and mantras, till they actually bring on illness. After awakening, they know that mind is Buddha, Buddha is mind; to recite the Buddha is to recite the mind; to recite the mind is to recite Buddha. Reciting Buddha from thought to thought is awakening the original mind from thought to thought — what is called mind and Buddha meeting in the Way, fused into one piece. Hence the ancients said, only after seeing the nature can one lift the single phrase of the Buddha's name with its full force, because before awakening one neither knows where the recitation lands nor avoids giving rise to doubt at every step, and so does not obtain real benefit. After awakening, having recognized the root-origin of the mind, one may recite or not recite — there is no matter of reciting or not reciting; one neither clings to form to seek recitation nor avoids it and refuses to recite. All day long, naked and bare, free and at ease, following conditions without hindrance — only now can one truly be said to be successively continuing the pure thought, with not a single thought that is not a Buddha-thought.

Regarding the phrase “successive continuity of pure thought,” there is great learning in it. It is entirely the same as the preserving-and-nurturing effort after awakening in the Chan school, and it is the index of the recitation practitioner's course of cultivation. Not grudging the words, I will briefly discuss it below.

The two words “pure thought” are not, as the common run of people imagine, merely reciting the Buddha with a pure mind; rather, when the recitation is mature, the mind that recites and the Buddha that is recited fall away at once, subject and object both vanish, and emptiness and existence are both extinguished — this right thought alone is called pure thought.

As for “successive continuity,” it is further distinguished by the depth of the practice into continuity in stillness, continuity in movement, and the unity of stillness and movement. Let me analyze as follows.

1. Continuity in stillness. When a recitation practitioner recites to the point where subject and object both vanish and the nature manifests itself, this is the first manifestation of pure thought. Thereafter, because the marks and habits accumulated over the beginningless kalpas are deep, it cannot appear in every sitting, but must be separated by several weeks, months, or even a year before it appears again; this all depends on the practitioner's faculties and the density of his practice. At this point the practitioner must redouble his diligence, so that the interval gradually shortens — from a year to several months, then a month, then several days, and finally it appears in every sitting. This is continuity in stillness, corresponding to the first stage of the Chan school's “preserving (bao)” effort; it is principle-and-mind single-mindedness.

2. Continuity in movement. When one can be continuously within stillness, yet when encountering the turmoil of states and conditions it is again interrupted, it cannot be called true continuity. One must train in the midst of daily activity, until one is free and unobstructed in every direction, unconstrained by favorable and adverse, as if in stillness, still solitary and luminous, without a single slip — only then is it continuity in movement. But if one occasionally forgets, and on meeting a state one stirs, immediately one is aware and returns to emptiness. This corresponds to the second stage of the “preserving (bao)” effort; it is practice-and-mind single-mindedness.

3. Unity of stillness and movement. Whether in movement or in stillness, there is no slipping, and moreover no mind of keeping — purely letting nature take its course. This corresponds to the first stage of the Chan school's “letting go (ren)” effort; it is principle-and-practice single-mindedness.

4. Even continuity is unobtainable, and the mind of not-keeping is likewise gone; all the former mysteries and wonders are swept away at once, and all day long one is as if foolish and dull, tasteless; yet within the tastelessness there is an utmost flavor. This corresponds to the second stage of the “letting go (ren)” effort; it is the single-mindedness of relating to all things. This is true successive continuity of pure thought.

For the convenience of later students in choosing a method of practice, I will extract the ten methods of cultivation spoken of by the Elder Zhine of the Yuan era, and present them for everyone's reference.

Question: I do not understand, in the teaching lineage, what Dharma is used to govern the mind? Answer: Use the mind of no-mind to govern the false mind. Question: If a person has no mind, he is then the same as grass and trees. Please, for the saying “no-mind,” grant me an expedient explanation. Answer: What is now called “no-mind” is not that there is no mind-substance, which is then called no-mind; rather, when there is nothing in the mind, it is called no-mind. For example, an empty bottle: because there is nothing in the bottle, it is called an empty bottle — not that there is no bottle-substance, which is then called an empty bottle. Hence the patriarch said: You have only to be without affairs in the mind and without mind in affairs, then naturally empty and yet numinous, still and yet wondrous — this is the essential purport of this mind. According to this, then it is the removing of the false mind, not the absence of the true mind's wondrous function. From of old the various masters have spoken of the practice of no-mind, each in different ways; now I will gather the main points and briefly set out ten kinds.

1. Awareness (juecha). That is, when practicing, ordinarily be free of thoughts and guard against the arising of thoughts; when a single thought is just born, immediately break it with awareness — the previous thought being broken by awareness, the later thought does not arise. This awareness-wisdom also need not be used; false and awareness alike are forgotten — this is called no-mind. Hence the patriarch said: Do not fear the arising of thought; only fear that awareness be slow. And a verse says: Do not seek the truth; only cease your views. This is the practice of awareness that stills false thought.

2. Rest (xiuxi). That is, when practicing, think neither of good nor of evil; when the mind rises, let it rest; when one meets conditions, let it be still. Hence it is said: Go on like a single strip of white silk, go on cold and chilly, go on like the incense-burner in an old temple! Only when you have eliminated all fineness and separation, foolish and dull, do you have a little correspondence. This is the practice of resting the false mind.

3. Extinguishing the mind and preserving the state (minxin cunjing). That is, when practicing, when all false thoughts are stilled, do not heed the external states, but simply still your own mind. The false mind being stilled, what harm are the external states? This is the ancient's method of robbing the person but not the state. Pang the Layman said: Only be without mind toward the ten thousand things — what harm if the ten thousand things always surround you! This is the practice of extinguishing thought, stilling the false, and preserving the state.

4. Extinguishing the state and preserving the mind (minjing cunxin). That is, when practicing, observe all the internal and external states as empty and still, preserving only the single mind, solitary and upright, standing alone. Hence the ancients said: Do not be a companion to the ten thousand things, do not make a counterpart to the dusts; if the mind attaches to a state, then the mind itself is false — now since there is no state, what falsehood is there? This is the ancient's method of robbing the state but not the person. Hence it is said: The flowers of the upper garden have already fallen, while the chariots and horses still crowd and throng. This is the practice of extinguishing the state, preserving the mind, and stilling the false.

5. Extinguishing both mind and state (minxin minjing). That is, when practicing, first empty the external states, then extinguish the inner mind; since internal and external, mind and state, are both still, in the end whence does the false arise? Hence Guanxi said: The ten directions have no wall to lean on, and the four sides have no gate. This is the patriarch's method of robbing both the person and the state. Hence the saying: The clouds scatter, the waters flow away; the person is still, heaven and earth are empty! This is the practice of extinguishing mind and state and stilling the false.

6. Preserving both state and mind (cunjing cunxin). That is, when practicing, let the mind abide in its position and the state abide in its position. Sometimes when mind and state face each other, the mind does not run toward the state, the state does not approach the mind; each not reaching the other, naturally false thoughts do not arise, and one is without hindrance to the Way. Hence the sutra says: This Dharma abides in its Dharma-position; the marks of the world abide everlastingly. This is the patriarch's method of robbing neither the person nor the state. Hence the saying: A single moon rises over the sea, and several families go up the tower! This is the practice of preserving state and mind and extirpating the false.

7. The whole body within and without (neiwai quanti). That is, when practicing, mountains, rivers, the great earth, sun, moon and stars, the inner body and outer vessels, all the dharmas — are the same as the true-mind substance, serene and void and bright, without a hair's difference; the great chiliocosm of worlds of dust fused into one piece — where could one still obtain a false mind! Hence Master Zhao said: Heaven and earth share the same root with me; the ten thousand dharmas are of the same substance as I. This is the practice of the whole body within and without, extirpating the false.

8. The complete function within and without (neiwai quanyong). That is, when practicing, observe all the inner and outer body and mind, vessels and realms, all dharmas, and all functions and activities, as the wondrous function of the true mind; when all thoughts are just born, that is the wondrous function manifest. Since everything is wondrous function, where could the false mind take its seat? Hence Yongjia said: The real nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is the Dharma-body. This is the practice of the complete function within and without, stilling the false.

9. Substance is function, function is substance (jiti jiyong). That is, when practicing, though one is fused with the true substance, of one flavor of emptiness and stillness, yet within it there is hidden a numinous clarity — the substance is the function; within the numinous clarity there is hidden emptiness and stillness — the function is the substance. Hence Yongjia said: Alert and tranquil is right; alert and falsely attached is wrong. Tranquil and alert is right; tranquil and indeterminate is wrong. Since in the midst of tranquility the indeterminate is not allowed, and in alertness chaotic thought is not used, how can any false mind arise? This is the practice of substance-is-function, function-is-substance, extirpating the false.

10. Breaking through substance and function (touchu tiyong). That is, when practicing, do not distinguish within and without, and do not distinguish east, west, south, north; take all the four directions and eight quarters as a single great gate of liberation. Round and full, substance and function not divided, without a hair's leakage, the whole body fused into one piece. Where could the false arise? The ancients said: The whole body is without seam or gap, above and below forming a round — this is the practice of breaking through substance and function, extirpating the false.

Of the above ten kinds of practice, one need not do them all; if one achieves a single gate, the false will naturally be stilled and the true mind appear. According to the root conditions of one's past lives with which some dharma has affinity, practice it accordingly. This practice is the practice of no-work, not a work that is done with the mind's contrivance. Even if one practices them without having awakened the true mind, it is easy to see it at once. This method of stilling the false mind is most important for those who study the Way; hence, not disliking detail, I record it to show later students. Do not regard it as gilding the lily!

The above ten practices are all to be exerted in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; one must be in dressing and eating, in relieving oneself, in conversation and work, in every moment and every place, closely and subtly aware and observant, without the need for sitting meditation and investigating. If there are those whose habits and obstruction are deep and whose strength is insufficient, and who still need to sit in meditation, let them continue as they wish; but after rising from the seat, they should carry the meditative power onto the states and train it in movement, so that they may sooner fuse it into one piece, and reach the great work of no-work, perfecting the great Way of bodhi.

As for the esoteric school, after awakening one must still practice esoterically, in order to attain realization in this very body. The breadth of its methods and the numerousness of its expedients far surpass the exoteric school. But the esoteric Dharma values a master's transmission and abhiseka; it cannot be openly displayed, so I shall omit it.

blocks.text: 4. Realizing the Essence and Activating Its Function
(1) The States of Realizing the Essence

inline.s: As for the states of realizing the essence, the ancients for the most part did not speak fully. First, because this realization-state is beyond the reach of words and thought; as soon as it falls into verbal expression it is guilty of dwelling. Second, because one who truly realizes it returns to having nothing attained, and does not wish to show it off to others. Third, for fear that those who have not awakened might steal it for themselves and so delude others. Fourth, for fear that people might attach to the state and seek it, thereby obstructing the gate of awakening. Fifth, because the states passed through by each person are not entirely the same. For these various reasons, they only sketched it with words like “the clouds disperse, the long sky fully revealed,” “the clear sky without a single cloud for ten thousand li,” “the mind-moon solitary and round, its light containing all things,” “neither light nor dark, neither great nor small, neither blue nor yellow,” or even “round and round, bright and brilliant.” I now seem to be no exception; and moreover I have nothing realized, nothing attained, and am even less able to speak. I can only pick up a few ready-made kung-an sayings to offer the readers. As for the detailed circumstances, I leave them for the reader to strive, realize, and experience himself.

When we practice until subject and object are both forgotten, and mind and Dharma both extinguished — no matter what school we cultivate — then it is a sudden snap and a sudden burst, like an explosive suddenly detonating: within, body and mind; without, the world; and even space itself, all at once fall away and are shattered into nothing, even that “nothing” is nothing. This is what is called the great earth sinking flat (vanishing) and space being shattered. At that very time, though there is not a single thing possessed, yet it is void-bright, still and coagulated, with a single numinous awareness not extinguished, clearly knowing, not like wood or stone. And though it is clear, yet there is neither that which knows nor that which is known; because this clarity is entirely one single mass of void-bright numinous knowing, there can no longer be a knower and a known — for there to be further knowledge would be adding a head upon a head, and would no longer be this. After we realize this true state, turning back, we then recognize that this “numinous knowing” is nowhere else — all day long it shines from the gate of the six sense-roots, without the slightest separation or gap from us; all our speech, movement, and activity is nothing but its numinous, wondrous function. Formerly we went through a thousand hardships and a hundred kinds of seeking and searching; it was all along right before our eyes but unrecognized — and instead we defiled it, humiliated it, revolving in the six realms, suffering — is that not a wrong and a sorrow! The ancients said: “The phrase before the sound, the thousand sages do not transmit; the single thread before the eye, from ancient times without a seam.” And again: “Having worn out iron shoes in seeking it without finding, when found it costs not a single effort.” This is what they point to.

〔The note “the phrase before the sound, the thousand sages do not transmit” — “the phrase before the sound” refers to the phrase before the sound is uttered, the phrase before father and mother gave birth to us; this is the Buddha and patriarchs' “treasury of the true Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of nirvana.” “The thousand sages” refers to the Buddhas and patriarchs who appeared in the past. It means that this “treasury of the true Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of nirvana” is neither a word nor a phrase, and could not be transmitted even by a thousand Buddhas and ten thousand patriarchs. It represents the great matter of the upward vehicle, which no one else can transmit, but which must be personally realized and attained through one's own realization. The Biyan Lu (Blue Cliff Record) says: “The phrase before the sound — the thousand sages do not transmit; never having personally seen it, it is as far as a great chiliocosm away.”

But this is only the plain Dharma-body; one must still diligently polish and grind, closely removing habits, before it can blaze forth in great light. When the practice is mature, even in deep sleep the crown of the head is bright with a full moon shining. When the light is pure and clear, the broad heavenly eye naturally opens, the ten directions world simultaneously illuminate, and I enter into all and all enter into me, like Indra's net, interpenetrating layer upon layer, with endless wondrous function.

Someone might say: Such states are realized by practitioners of the Chan or esoteric schools; followers of the Pure Land school who recite the Buddha's name should not be so, for they aim at rebirth in the Western Pure Land, and ought in concentration to see Amitabha Buddha and the Western sacred states, and should not be utterly without seeing. If one sees nothing at all, how can one be reborn in the Pure Land?

Answer: Have you not seen the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi of Master Yinguang recorded above? Master Yinguang is one who vigorously advocates relying on the Buddha's compassionate power to be received and led to rebirth in the West. Why then does he also say, in the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi, that no-seeing is true seeing, and that true seeing has nothing seen? Because the true Thusness Buddha-nature is without form or mark, unstained by a single dust, unsullied by a single thread; to say it is like any one thing is already not right. Hence the true Buddha truly has nothing to be said and no form to be seen. But this formless Buddha-nature is not blank nothingness; hence it can follow conditions to manifest marks and put forth function. But because the marks arise following conditions, they are only provisional names, not a real substance. Hence to see a Buddha with marks is not to see the true Buddha. The ancients said: The reward- and transformation-bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they the expounders of the Dharma. The Lotus Sutra calls them a phantom city, not the jewel-mansion. Those who wish a highest-grade, highest rebirth in the Western Pure Land must pass through the small resting-place of forms, and realize the true Buddha's markless wondrous body, before they can fulfill their wish. Conversely, clinging to a Buddha with form and a Pure Land with marks can only yield the lowest-grade rebirth; this is an immutable truth. Hence Master Yinguang, when speaking of the highest state of Buddha-recitation — the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi — could not but say that seeing-without-seeing is true seeing. For having realized such a profound and lofty state, mind and land are fused into one piece; mind is the land, the land is mind. To make the vow for rebirth in the West is just to be reborn in the Pure Land of one's own mind — to be reborn without a birth — and would one still fear not having the highest-grade rebirth?
